title: Rich Georgians Wore Dentures Pulled From Dead Soldiers' Mouths
description: AI-narrated commentary on the real, documented 19th-century trade in dead soldiers' teeth used to make dentures -- 'Waterloo teeth,' George Washington's actual dentures, and how the practice continued for decades. Original commentary, not a reused clip.

hook_candidates.text: Dead soldiers' mouths supplied Georgian England's most expensive smile.
Where do you think rich Georgians actually got their perfect smile?
George Washington's teeth weren't wood. They came from someone else's mouth.
In 1815, scavengers walked Waterloo's battlefield with pliers, not muskets.

share_trigger: A viewer sends this to the friend who's terrified of the dentist, because they want to prove today's checkup is nothing compared to Georgian dentures.
contradicted_belief: Most people assume old-timey dentures were carved from wood or ivory, not pulled from dead soldiers' mouths.
closing_comment: Georgians really paid extra for dentures pulled from dead soldiers, and most had no idea.

sources.note: Confirms scavengers pulled teeth from Waterloo's dead, sold to London dentists as 'Waterloo teeth.'
Confirms Washington's dentures were ivory and human teeth, not wood, debunking the wooden-teeth myth.
Confirms Civil War battlefield teeth were harvested and shipped to Europe, continuing the earlier trade.
